paraphrase: Chapter on abandoning the belief in permanence: one who has the three worlds' lord of death as his master should not sleep as if he were immortal; since all who are born must die, clinging to the impermanent as permanent brings grief, and seeing death clearly one turns from craving.
notes: Chapter-level summary from memory; the opening image of the lord of death to be checked.

paraphrase: Chapter refuting the self: a permanent self could neither act nor be harmed, so non-harm would be meaningless; the self cannot be the body, the mind or apart from them, and what is called 'I' arises only through ignorance, as a snake is imputed to a rope.
notes: Chapter-level summary; the ahiṃsā argument (10.x) and rope-snake gloss seen in the local e-text of Candrakīrti's ṭīkā (ch.10), verse numbers not fixed.

paraphrase: One who is impartial, intelligent and eager is called a vessel for hearing; otherwise neither the speaker's nor the hearer's qualities bear fruit.
notes: The local e-text's first word is corrupt ('śaṅkuṣṭha'); 'impartial' (madhyastha) follows the Tibetan understanding.

paraphrase: The Tathāgatas describe the Dharma, in brief, as non-harming, and emptiness alone as nirvāṇa; here there are only these two.

original.text: dharmaṃ samāsato'hiṃsāṃ varṇayanti tathāgatāḥ | śūnyatāmeva nirvāṇaṃ kevalaṃ tadihobhayam ||

paraphrase: One who has no position — 'existent', 'non-existent' or 'both existent and non-existent' — cannot be refuted even over a long time.

paraphrase: First turning away from demerit, in the middle turning away from the self, afterwards turning away from everything — whoever knows this is wise.

paraphrase: Just as a barbarian cannot be made to understand in another language, so the world cannot be made to understand without the worldly.
